H1.text: Press the spring in a pen, and it pushes back. Sit on a sofa, and its springs push you up.

H2.text: A squeezed spring can do work. So it must be storing energy.

H3.text: Aarav loads his toy spring gun. He pushes the ball in, and the spring gets shorter.

H4.text: He pulls the trigger, and the ball shoots across the room. Where was that energy hiding, and how much was there?

H5.text: By the end of this video, you will work it out in joules.

P1.text: So what is the potential energy of a spring?

P2.text: Stretch or squeeze a spring, and it pulls or pushes back, towards its normal length.

P3.text: The further you stretch it, the harder it pulls. Twice the stretch, twice the force.

P4.text: This is Hooke's law. F equals minus k x. k is the spring constant, in newtons per metre.

P5.text: The work you do to stretch it is stored in the spring. That is its potential energy.

S1.text: Let's run it. An eight kilogram block on a smooth floor, tied to a spring. k is two hundred newtons per metre.

S2.text: Pull it ten centimetres to the right. The spring pulls back with twenty newtons.

S3.text: Pull to twenty centimetres. Now it pulls back with forty newtons. Double.

S4.text: On the graph, the force grows in a straight line. The work is the area under it, a triangle.

S5.text: At twenty centimetres, the area is half, times zero point two, times forty. Four joules stored.

S6.text: Now let go. The spring pulls the block back, and the stored energy becomes speed.

S7.text: Slow-mo replay, as it passes the middle.

S8.text: In the middle, the spring is at its normal length. The force is zero, U is zero, and the speed is the largest.

D1.text: Now the formula, step by step.

D2.text: Step one. To stretch it slowly, your pull must match the spring. F equals k x.

D3.text: Step two. The force grows from zero to k x. So we cannot just multiply force by distance.

D4.text: Step three. The work is the area under the force graph. A triangle, with base x and height k x.

D5.text: Step four. The area is half, times x, times k x. Half k x squared.

D6.text: Step five. That work is stored. U equals half k x squared, whether you stretch it or squeeze it.

T1.text: Remember this. A spring stretched or squeezed by x stores half k x squared.

R1.text: Why x squared, and not just x? Follow the links.

R2.text: One. Double the stretch, and the final force doubles.

R3.text: Two. The distance you pull also doubles.

R4.text: Three. So the triangle is twice as wide and twice as tall. Its area is four times bigger.

R5.text: Four. Double the stretch, four times the energy. Triple it, nine times.

C2.text: Stretch the spring by ten centimetres. U is half, times two hundred, times zero point one squared. One joule.

C3.text: Squeeze it by ten centimetres. x is minus zero point one, but its square is the same. One joule again.

C4.text: Now you try. Spring A is stiff, k is four hundred. Spring B is soft, k is one hundred. Same pull on both. Which stores more energy? Pause and decide.

C5.text: The soft one! With the same force, it stretches four times as far. U is F squared over two k.

C6.text: One more. Is the spring force conservative? Pause and think.

C7.text: Yes! Stretch it and let it come back, and the spring's total work is zero. That is why it has a potential energy.

W2.text: Aarav's gun spring has k equal to four hundred newtons per metre. He squeezes it five centimetres, and fires a twenty gram ball. How fast does it leave?

W3.text: First, units. Zero point zero five metres, and zero point zero two kilograms.

W4.text: Stored energy. Half, times four hundred, times zero point zero five squared. Zero point five joules.

W5.text: All of it becomes kinetic energy. Half, times zero point zero two, times v squared, equals zero point five.

W6.text: So v squared is fifty. v is about seven point zero seven metres per second.

X2.text: Many students say the work to stretch a spring is force times stretch, k x times x.

X3.text: But the force grows from zero. Use the triangle: half k x squared. And always put x in metres.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In spring numericals: a block hits a spring, or the work between two stretches.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A spring with k equal to eight hundred newtons per metre is already stretched by five centimetres. How much more work is needed to stretch it to ten centimetres? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Three joules.

A2.text: At ten centimetres, U is half, times eight hundred, times zero point one squared. Four joules.

A3.text: At five centimetres, U is half, times eight hundred, times zero point zero five squared. One joule.

A4.text: The extra work is four minus one. Three joules.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why is the energy half k x squared, and not k x squared?

Y3.text: Two. Double the stretch. What happens to the stored energy?

Y4.text: Three. Does a squeezed spring store energy too?

N1.text: Next time: swing a bucket of water over your head, and not a drop falls. Find out how in motion in a vertical circle.
